title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
subtitle: The Terms of Peace, Painful Compromise, and Deep Wisdom
summary: The arrival of Suhayl ibn Amr, the Prophet erasing his own title for the sake of peace, the ten-year truce, the heartbreaking return of Abu Jandal in iron chains, Umar's agonizing questions and Abu Bakr's steadfastness, and Umm Salamah's brilliant counsel.

sections.text: The Arrival of Suhayl ibn Amr

Shaken by the resolute oath of Bay'at al-Ridwan, the Makkan leadership realized that the Muslims would neither retreat in humiliation nor be easily broken. They dispatched their most articulate statesman, Suhayl ibn Amr, with strict instructions to negotiate a formal treaty that preserved Makkan pride by turning the Muslims back this year. When the Prophet ﷺ saw Suhayl approaching, he perceived a positive divine omen in his name (Suhayl deriving from 'Sahl', meaning ease), remarking to his companions: 'Your affair has now become easy.'
Drafting the Treaty & The Erased Words

The Prophet called Ali ibn Abi Talib to write down the agreement. The Prophet dictated: 'Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim).' Suhayl objected bluntly: 'As for "Ar-Rahman", by Allah, I do not know what it is! Rather, write what we customary use: "In Your Name, O Allah (Bismikallahumma)".' The companions protested, but the Prophet gently instructed Ali: 'Write: Bismikallahumma.'

The Prophet continued: 'This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed upon with Suhayl ibn Amr.' Suhayl protested again: 'By Allah, if we believed you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have barred you from the House nor fought you! Rather, write: Muhammad ibn Abdillah.' Ali hesitated, saying: 'By Allah, my hand will never erase your title of Messenger of Allah!' The Prophet took the parchment, asked Ali to point out the words, and erased them with his own hand, writing 'Muhammad ibn Abdillah'—demonstrating sublime humility for the sake of higher peace.

The agreed terms stipulated: a complete ten-year armistice (Hudnah) between the two parties; freedom for any Arabian tribe to enter into an alliance with either Muhammad or Quraysh; the Muslims would return to Madinah this year without entering Makkah, but would be permitted to perform Umrah the following year for three days carrying only sheathed swords; and a controversial extradition clause stating that any person escaping from Quraysh to Muhammad without his guardian's permission must be returned to Makkah, whereas anyone fleeing from Muhammad to Quraysh would not be returned.

Just as the ink was drying on the parchment, Abu Jandal, the son of the negotiator Suhayl himself, appeared staggering into the camp dragging heavy iron fetters on his feet. He had escaped imprisonment in Makkah and thrown himself before the Muslims pleading for sanctuary. Suhayl stood up and struck his son across the face, shouting: 'O Muhammad! The agreement between us was concluded before this boy arrived; he is the first person you must return to me under the treaty!'

The companions gasped in distress. The Prophet pleaded with Suhayl to grant Abu Jandal to him as a personal favor, but Suhayl stubbornly refused. The Prophet comforted Abu Jandal with profound faith: 'O Abu Jandal! Be patient and seek reward from Allah, for Allah will surely make for you and those oppressed with you a relief and an escape. We have concluded a treaty of peace and given our word, and we cannot betray our word.' Abu Jandal was led away in chains, weeping, while the hearts of the companions burned with grief.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, shaken by what seemed like humiliating concessions, went to the Prophet ﷺ asking: 'Are you not truly the Messenger of Allah? Are we not upon truth and our enemy upon falsehood?' The Prophet replied with absolute calm: 'Yes, I am the Messenger of Allah, and I do not disobey Him, and He will never forsake me.' Umar then went to Abu Bakr, asking the exact same questions. Abu Bakr, without having heard the Prophet's response, gave the identical reply: 'Hold fast to his stirrup, for he is indeed the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never forsake him.' Later in life, Umar performed extensive voluntary fasting, prayer, and charity to expiate for his questioning on that day.

When the treaty was finalized, the Prophet commanded the companions: 'Arise, sacrifice your animals, and shave your heads.' Stunned by the disappointment of not entering the Ka'bah, no one moved. The Prophet repeated the command three times, yet silence reigned. Grieved, he entered the tent of his wife Umm Salamah and confided in her. Umm Salamah gave counsel of legendary wisdom: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not speak a word to anyone; go out, sacrifice your camel, and call your barber to shave your head in their sight.'

The Prophet followed her advice. When the companions saw him sacrificing his camel and shaving his hair, the spiritual fog lifted. They rushed forward, sacrificing their animals and shaving one another's heads with such urgency that they nearly injured each other in remorse. A treaty that outwardly appeared as compromise was about to reveal itself as the greatest victory in Arabian history.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah Al-Fath (48:24–27)
references.notes: Divine wisdom explaining why battle was restrained at Hudaybiyyah to protect secret believers in Makkah.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.source: Kitab al-Shurut, Bab al-Shurut fi al-Jihad, Hadith 2731–2732
references.notes: Bukhari 2731–2732 includes Suhayl's terms, the erasure of the heading, Abu Jandal, and Umm Salamah's advice to the Prophet to go out and sacrifice. The citation is that narration.

references.title: Sahih Muslim
references.author: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 261 AH)
references.source: Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar, the treaty of Hudaybiyyah
references.notes: Umar's distress at the terms is part of the long Hudaybiyyah narration. Muslim 1785 was not re-opened separately, so the old span 1783–1785 is not asserted number by number.
